steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a computer vision paper on estimating extreme 3D relative rotations between pairs of images with little or no overlap, using Transformer cross-attention. Cover the background and classical approaches, our method and its parts, what we observe in experiments, and a list of contributions.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Estimating the relative pose between two images is an important task in computer vision. It is used in many applications such as indoor navigation, augmented reality, autonomous driving, 3D reconstruction, camera localization, simultaneous localization and mapping, and novel view synthesis. The current way of doing image registration is to extract features, match them and establish correspondence between them. But this does not work for input pairs with little or no overlap, like the images in Fig. 1, because then it is hard to get enough feature correspondences for matching.

Many applications need an accurate estimate of the rotations between images. For extreme 3D rotation estimation between images with limited or no overlap, as in Fig. 1, the common approach goes back to the seminal work of Coughlan and Yuille. Their technique is based on linear structures in an image, which mostly come from three mutually orthogonal directions, one vertical (building walls) and two horizontal (ground pavements, roads, etc.). In a similar way, "Single View Metrology" by Criminisi et al. and its extensions use parallel image lines and the corresponding vanishing points to calibrate the camera. Relative camera rotation can also be estimated from illumination cues, by looking at the directions of lighting and shadows.

In this work we propose a deep-learning approach to estimate large, extreme rotations between images. Classical formulations explicitly detect hand-crafted cues such as lines, shadows and vanishing points, but our method regresses the relative rotation directly from the input images with a deep neural network. We were inspired by the recent successful use of Transformers in computer vision tasks such as object detection and image recognition, and we adapt Transformers for several tasks in our pipeline, shown in Fig. 2, which goes further than the previous applications of Transformers.

- Three uses of Transformers
  - Transformers-Decoders: cross-decoding, each embedding queries the other's
  - Transformer-Encoder: stacked multihead attention, cross-attention between latent representations; improves on 4DCV (inner products, single layer of N^{2} inner products)
  - cascade of two decoders + learnt rotation query, refined jointly
  - general-purpose (optical flow, registration, relative pose regression); other applications = future work
- Observations and evaluation
  - attention maps (Section 3.2) highlight vertical / horizontal lines
  - SOTA on non-overlapping pairs; end-to-end, regression loss
  - StreetLearn, SUN360, InteriorNet; overlap classes, indoor/outdoor, varying illumination; Section 4
- Contributions
  - extreme rotation scheme incl. minimal overlap
  - cross-decoding of embeddings
  - Transformer-Encoder cross-attention
  - decoder-decoder module, quaternionic rotation queries
  - favorable results on indoor and outdoor datasets

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Estimating the relative pose between two images is an important task in computer vision. It is used in many applications such as indoor navigation, augmented reality, autonomous driving, 3D reconstruction, camera localization, simultaneous localization and mapping, and novel view synthesis. The current way of doing image registration is to extract features, match them and establish correspondence between them. But this does not work for input pairs with little or no overlap, like the images in Fig. 1, because then it is hard to get enough feature correspondences for matching.

Many applications need an accurate estimate of the rotations between images. For extreme 3D rotation estimation between images with limited or no overlap, as in Fig. 1, the common approach goes back to the seminal work of Coughlan and Yuille. Their technique is based on linear structures in an image, which mostly come from three mutually orthogonal directions, one vertical (building walls) and two horizontal (ground pavements, roads, etc.). In a similar way, "Single View Metrology" by Criminisi et al. and its extensions use parallel image lines and the corresponding vanishing points to calibrate the camera. Relative camera rotation can also be estimated from illumination cues, by looking at the directions of lighting and shadows.

In this work we propose a deep-learning approach to estimate large, extreme rotations between images. Classical formulations explicitly detect hand-crafted cues such as lines, shadows and vanishing points, but our method regresses the relative rotation directly from the input images with a deep neural network. We were inspired by the recent successful use of Transformers in computer vision tasks such as object detection and image recognition, and we adapt Transformers for several tasks in our pipeline, shown in Fig. 2, which goes further than the previous applications of Transformers.

First, we use Transformers-Decoders to improve the embeddings of the input images. They distill inter-image information by cross-decoding, where each embedding uses the embedding of the other image as a query, so the images are encoded better with respect to each other. Second, a Transformer-Encoder computes a stacked multihead attention to encode the cross-attention between the latent representations of the image pair. This is an improvement over the 4D correlation volume (4DCV) used in prior works, where the 4DCVs were computed by inner products. A 4DCV is a single layer of N^{2} inner products, while our Transformer-Encoder approach uses the more advanced architecture of multi-head attention to better encode the interactions between entries of the activation maps. Third, we improve the cross-attention encoding further with a cascade of two decoders and a learnt rotation query, which refines the cross-attention encoding and the rotation query jointly. The scheme is a general-purpose attention-based architecture for estimating attributes related to two input images, such as optical flow, registration, relative pose regression, etc. Our motivation was extreme rotation estimation, and we leave the other applications for future work since they will need more task-specific modifications.

Interestingly, the attention maps that our scheme computes (shown in Section 3.2) show that the Transformer-Encoder gives high attention scores to image regions with rotation-informative cues, especially vertical and horizontal lines. We also see that the approach can predict the rotation of non-overlapping image pairs with state-of-the-art (SOTA) accuracy. The framework is trainable end-to-end and optimizes a regression loss. We evaluate it on three dataset benchmarks, StreetLearn, SUN360 and InteriorNet, which have different overlap classes in indoor and outdoor locations and varying illumination. The experiments in Section 4 show that our model gets state-of-the-art (SOTA) accuracy.

Our contributions are the following.

- We propose a new scheme to estimate extreme rotations, including when the images barely overlap.

- We enhance the image embeddings with cross-decoding, which distills inter-image information.

- We propose a Transformer-Encoder cross-attention mechanism to encode the interactions in latent space between the image pairs.

- A decoder-decoder module infers the relative rotation from the cross-attention encoding, by learning and applying quaternionic rotation queries.

- Quantitative evaluations show that we compare favorably with state-of-the-art rotation estimation techniques on indoor and outdoor datasets.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Estimating the relative pose between a pair of images is a crucial task in computer vision, used in various applications such as indoor navigation, augmented reality, autonomous driving, 3D reconstruction [1,2], camera localization [3,4,5], simultaneous localization and mapping [6,7], and novel view synthesis [8,9]. The current approach to image registration involves extracting features, matching them, and establishing correspondence between them. However, this approach is ineffective for input pairs with little or no overlap, such as the images shown in Fig. 1, as it is difficult to establish sufficient feature correspondences for matching.

Numerous applications [10,11,12] require precise estimation of inter-image rotations. The prevalent approach for extreme 3D rotation estimation between images with limited or no overlap, as in Fig. 1, relates to the seminal work of Coughlan and Yuille [13], who introduced a technique based on linear structures within an image, primarily arising from three mutually orthogonal directions - one vertical (building walls) and two horizontal (ground pavements, roads, etc.). Similarly, "Single View Metrology" by Criminisi et al. [14] and its extensions [15,16,17] use parallel image lines and corresponding vanishing points [18] for camera calibration. Relative camera rotation can also be estimated via illumination cues [19], by analyzing lighting and shadow directions.

In this work, we propose a deep-learning approach for estimating significant, extreme inter-image rotations. Unlike classical formulations [13,14] that explicitly detect hand-crafted cues such as lines, shadows, and vanishing points, our method directly regresses the relative rotation from the input images using a deep neural network. Inspired by recent successful applications of Transformers [20] in computer vision tasks such as object detection [21] and image recognition [22], we adapt Transformers for multiple tasks within the proposed pipeline shown in Fig. 2, going beyond previous applications of Transformers.

First, we apply Transformers-Decoders to improve the input image embeddings by distilling inter-image information through cross-decoding, where each embedding uses the other's embedding as a query, so that the images are better encoded with respect to each other. Second, a Transformer-Encoder computes a stacked multihead attention to encode cross-attention between the latent representations of image pairs. This improves on the 4D correlation volume (4DCV) used in prior works [23,24,25,26,27], where 4DCVs were calculated by inner products: instead of a single layer of N^{2} inner products, the proposed Transformer-Encoder-based approach uses the more advanced architecture of multi-head attention to better encode interactions between activation map entries. Third, we further improve the cross-attention encoding using a cascade of two decoders and a learnt rotation query, jointly refining the cross-attention encoding and the rotation query. The proposed scheme is a general-purpose attention-based architecture for estimating attributes related to two input images, such as optical flow, registration, relative pose regression, etc. This work was motivated by extreme rotation estimation, and we leave other applications for future work, as they will require additional task-specific modifications.

Interestingly, the attention maps computed by our scheme, shown in Section 3.2, show that the Transformer-Encoder assigns high attention scores to image regions containing rotation-informative cues, emphasizing vertical and horizontal lines. We also observe that the proposed approach predicts the rotation of non-overlapping image pairs with state-of-the-art (SOTA) accuracy. Our framework is end-to-end trainable and optimizes a regression loss. It is evaluated on three dataset benchmarks, StreetLearn [28], SUN360 [29] and InteriorNet [30], with different overlap classes in indoor and outdoor locations and under varying illumination. The experimental results in Section 4 show that our model provides state-of-the-art (SOTA) accuracy.

In summary, our contributions are as follows.

- We propose a novel scheme for estimating extreme rotations, including scenarios with minimal image overlap.

- Image embeddings are enhanced through cross-decoding, which distills inter-image information.

- A Transformer-Encoder cross-attention mechanism is proposed to encode latent space interactions between image pairs.

- A decoder-decoder module infers the relative rotation from the cross-attention encoding by learning and applying quaternionic rotation queries.

- Quantitative evaluations show favorable performance compared to state-of-the-art rotation estimation techniques on indoor and outdoor datasets.
